summary: NFSv4 lets servers cooperate to provide an organization-wide file namespace. This RFC uses DNS SRV records so an organization can publish where the root of that namespace is, even for clients not closely tied to it, and so such namespaces can be joined together.

eli5.summary: The phone book can say which computer holds the main folder of an organization's files, so anyone can find it.

questions: how to find an nfsv4 server with dns srv

subtitle: Using a DNS SRV record to find the root of an organization's NFSv4 file tree.

tldr.problem: An organization using NFSv4 may want to publish the starting point of its file namespace to clients, even outsiders, while clients should need to know only a minimum, stable piece of information.
tldr.mechanism: The organization publishes DNS SRV records under _nfs-domainroot._tcp. Servers named there export the root at /.domainroot/{Name}, and clients mount it under a conventional directory such as /nfs4/.
tldr.outcome: A client needs only a domain name to find that domain's published file namespace, and namespaces can be joined into one global tree. The design relies on DNS integrity, so DNSSEC SHOULD be used.

today: RFC 6641 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this site lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on NFSv4 as defined in RFC 3530 and RFC 5661.

sections.title: Background
sections.content:
NFS version 4 (RFC 3530) introduced the fs_locations attribute, and NFSv4 minor version 1 (RFC 5661) added an extended form called fs_locations_info. These attributes work as referrals: a server tells its client that the tree below a given name lives on some other set of servers. With referrals, servers can cooperate to build a namespace that crosses server boundaries.

An organization might want to publish the starting point of such a namespace, perhaps to a broad set of clients. Clients should need to know as little as possible, and that information should stay constant over the life of the organization, even when a server's name or address changes.
sections.eli5: Many computers can share one big set of folders. People still need a simple way to learn where the top folder is, without memorizing which computer holds it.

sections.title: Finding the Root with DNS SRV
sections.content:
The RFC maps a DNS name to the NFS file systems that provide the root of that name's namespace. These are called domain root file systems. From there, a client navigates the rest of the namespace with ordinary NFS mechanisms. A client needs to know only the organization's domain name.

Servers are found with the DNS SRV record (RFC 2782), whose format is _Service._Proto.Name TTL Class SRV Priority Weight Port Target. The service name is _nfs-domainroot and the protocol name is _tcp. Other protocols MUST use another protocol name, and _udp MUST NOT be used to imply UDP with NFSv4, since neither RFC 3530 nor RFC 5661 defines NFSv4 over UDP. The Target fields name the servers that export the domain's root.

Those servers MUST export the root at /.domainroot/{Name} inside their pseudo-file systems, where Name is the organization name used in the SRV record. The service is not useful for NFS versions before 4, because fs_locations first appeared in NFSv4.
sections.eli5: You look up the organization's name in the phone book and it lists the computers that hold the top folder. Each entry also says which door number to knock on.

sections.title: A Worked Example
sections.content:
For the organization example.net, the DNS servers would publish these records:

_nfs-domainroot._tcp IN SRV 0 0 2049 nfs1tr.example.net.
_nfs-domainroot._tcp IN SRV 1 0 18204 nfs2ex.example.net.

The names nfs1tr.example.net and nfs2ex.example.net are NFSv4 servers that export the root of the published namespace. Priority and Weight are interpreted as in RFC 2782 to pick a server. Both servers export the file system at /.domainroot/example.net, which clients mount. The first record uses port 2049, the port assigned to NFS, and the second uses a different port. Clients connect to each server on its listed port.
sections.eli5: The phone book lists two computers for example.net. One is the first choice and one is a backup, and each says which door to use.

sections.title: Client Integration
sections.content:
An NFSv4 client following this specification implements a special directory, like an automounter directory, whose entries are domain names that have recently been traversed. When an application tries to look up a new name there, the client consults DNS for the SRV data, and on success mounts the indicated file systems under that name. To the application, each entry looks like a directory holding the root of the file system published by that domain.

For the namespace to be global, the mount point must be the same on all clients. On POSIX machines the convention is /nfs4/, so example.net would appear as /nfs4/example.net/ on any POSIX client.

For the rootpath field of fs_location, or the fli_fs_root field of fs_locations_info, servers MUST use the /.domainroot/{Name} string. The client SHOULD NOT insist on a writable copy if read-only copies exist, or on a zero-age copy, because the default should cost the server as little as possible. The result of the DNS search SHOULD appear as a (pseudo-)directory, and only fully qualified domain names are RECOMMENDED to appear as directories. An abbreviated form SHOULD be a symbolic link to the fully qualified name.

The client does the interpreting, and it should cache the DNS result, obeying the Time to Live (TTL). The RFC does not define use of the SRV record with Multicast DNS: mDNS could locate only a local domain root, so it has too little value here.
sections.eli5: There is a special folder on your computer. When you open a folder named after a company, your computer quietly looks up where that company keeps its files and connects.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The design adds a new reliance of NFSv4 on the integrity of DNS. Forged SRV records could lead a client to an attacker's file servers instead of the organization's own. The RFC notes this is similar to attacks possible on base NFSv4 when server names are given in fs_location attributes.

If DNSSEC (RFC 4033) is available, it SHOULD be used. Domain-based service principal names (RFC 5178 and RFC 5179) are a further mechanism, and the RFC says it would be prudent to use them. The idea is to authenticate {nfs, domainname, host.fqdn} rather than just {nfs, host.fqdn}. For the second server in the example, the GSS-API name would be nfs@example.net@nfs2ex.example.net. The domain administrator can then make sure only domain root servers hold credentials for such names.

NFSv4 already negotiates security mechanisms, so this document does not describe that. Publishing SRV records may expose NFS servers to attacks, so organizations should consider whether their DNS servers should answer differently to clients inside and outside a given perimeter.
sections.eli5: If someone sneaks a fake entry into the phone book, you could end up at the wrong computer. So the entries should be signed, and you should check the computer really is the one it claims to be.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA assigned a new service name, nfs-domainroot, for TCP, with no associated port number, following RFC 6335. The assignee is the IESG and the reference is this document. The description is: NFS service for the domain root, the root of an organization's published file namespace.
sections.eli5: The official list of names now includes this one, so nobody else uses it for something different.
